text: Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao 7 October, 2026 in guest blog , opinion | Tags: AI , Association for Human Mathematics | by Terence Tao [This is a guest post by the Association for Human Mathematics , reposted from their statements page . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Yesterday, on October 6th, 2026, OpenAI — which is currently defending lawsuits against accusations of illegal plagiarism, copyright infringement, and trademark dilution — released a repository of manuscripts purporting to contain solutions to a number of high-profile problems in mathematics. Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, from whom OpenAI has claimed to derive its legitimacy, opened their initial advisory statement by saying that frontier AI corporations should not test advanced mathematical problems on internal models. In ignoring the central premise of the Advisory Group’s position, OpenAI has indicated total disregard for the norms of scientific research — norms that guarantee that mathematics remains trustworthy, ethically researched, and in the public interest. Mathematicians have a particular vision of progress that is informed by history and field-specific considerations. We reject OpenAI’s assertion that this release advances our subject, and we urge mathematicians and the public to view the value of this publication model with due skepticism. Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power. We urge mathematicians to discontinue their work with OpenAI and to return to a vision of science that centers human understanding. If we lived in a world where financial burdens weren’t imposed on mathematicians then we wouldn’t be here in the first place. 8 October, 2026 at 9:44 am geeksingularity The AHM statement raises fair concerns about process, but its central argument would not survive the standards it claims to defend. Mathematics has never asked whether a result was requested. It asks whether it is correct. “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done” is not a mathematical objection; it is a jurisdictional one. No field that prides itself on openness gets to decide who may attempt its problems. The statement leads with OpenAI’s unrelated lawsuits. Whatever their merits, they have no bearing on whether a single one of these 700 manuscripts is right or wrong. We would not accept that line of argument against a human author, and we should not accept it here. The claim that releasing 700 files is “a demonstration of power” rather than scholarship has it backwards. Publishing claimed proofs in full, where anyone can check them, is the most exposed position an author can take. If the arguments are flawed, the flaws are now in plain view. That is how mathematics has always kept itself trustworthy: not by restricting who may speak, but by checking what is said. The Advisory Group’s position deserves a hearing, but an advisory statement is not a norm of scientific research, and declining to follow it is not “total disregard” for those norms. The norms that actually matter here are verification, priority, and attribution. On those, there are legitimate questions to press: how the manuscripts were vetted, whether they come with formal verification, how prior human work is credited, and who bears the cost of refereeing at this volume. Those questions would make a strong statement. A call to boycott does not. Urging the public toward “due skepticism” is reasonable. But skepticism means reading the proofs and finding the errors. Urging mathematicians to stop working with OpenAI altogether asks them to stop looking, and that is the opposite of skepticism. If human understanding is the goal, the community’s best response is to engage: check the results, publish the refutations where they fail, and credit them where they hold. 8 October, 2026 at 11:27 am Anonymous The OpenAI lawsuits are not unrelated: They are about IP theft, and are as such relevant to potential plagiarism or lack of attribution in the proofs or IP theft through prompts. 9 October, 2026 at 7:59 am pascoej You wonder if people really hate math or these people are plants. 8 October, 2026 at 10:39 am William Oliver I want to reply in bulk to the lay people who think that this is a kind of ‘gatekeeping’ and who believe that mathematicians are not doing a good job of explaining why they are reacting this way. Well, personally, I do not agree that it’s gatekeeping, but I do think this is quite a fair response. I do not think mathematicians have done a great job of communicating the problems related to AI and mathematics and why humans are important for mathematical practice. I think to simply dismiss the laypeople who think this is the case is unreasonable. That said, this statement from the AHM is based on a real concern: this isn’t mathematicians simply ‘whining’ about it. So, until we get a more ‘organized’ explanation, for now, let me attempt to try to explain what exactly the problem is here as I see it personally. There are 3 main points I can make, and the third is the most important (and the longest, because its hardest to describe). [ For non-laypeople : I also would like to say that the philosophical position presented in the third part of this may be useful to mathematicians in this crisis. This is as formal as I will get about it in this comment, but I just want to try to lend some legitimacy to the ideas I am expositing. It presents a definition of Kant’s ‘regulative ideas’ as a proposition that is necessarily possible in the sense of modal logic, which relates this to classical logic through the Fitting-Smullyan intuitionistic interpretation of classical logic (and forcing) as the logic one gets when one considers what is (recursively) necessarily possible in an S4 Kripke Frame. This then has implications on a more ‘harmonious’ interpretation of intuitionistic logic’s relationship with classical logic. In particular, intuitionists, I think, although inspired by Immanuel Kant’s philosophy, missed the incorporation of one of his best ideas (the idea that metaphysical or ontological beliefs play an essential regulatory role in the acquisition of knowledge). And so, I am arguing that this regulatory aspect of the mind is a specific, practical, formal, faculty that will remain something that Artificial Intelligence cannot replicate without the active help of human beings. And I think amounts to a kind of ‘Mathematical Idealism’ that is separate from other common positions on the philosophy of mathematics such as platonism or intuitionism. I would like to emphasize though that this is mostly a comment for laypeople] Now back to the 3 main points: I think there is a very simple question to start with. What does it actually mean for a theorem to be true? And suppose we know that a theorem is true, why is it that true theorems that at first appear to have no practical application end up being helpful to humanity? Before I continue, its very important to emphasize this point: this is now a statement that is not only about the abstract realm of mathematics, but about the physical world , since we can actually build this machine and run it. The first question is: is it true that the program/agent either ends its search or doesn’t? (Again, remembering that this is a question at least partially about the physical world) If you believe the answer is yes, then assuming that there are no inconsistencies in Lean, then we have just shown that truth is not the same as formal validity. We do not have to know which answer is actually the case to draw this conclusion, just that it is either one or the other. But many might say that the answer is no (i.e. there is no truth value here). In other words, you have to be committed to the fact that in reality the AI neither ceases its search nor searches endlessly. This may be true, but it is an entirely different philosophical can of worms. In other words: again, we are making this claim about physical reality , not just about an abstract realm of mathematical truths. And so the question is, under this view, do you actually believe this? The belief that all statements are either true or false is called the “Law of the excluded middle”. And its rejection is the defining feature of a kind of logic called Intuitionistic logic which, incidentally, is what a lot of proof assistant languages like Lean are based on. Whether or not you believe it one way or another, I think this is the quickest way to show a layperson the general ‘feeling’ of the difference between understanding and formal proof, and perhaps the difference between truth and a formal proof. We have an ‘understanding’ that the program will either halt or it won’t, but a) we can’t prove it and b) if we think we don’t need to prove it, then it implies there is a statement that is true but not provable. There are some standard objections to the idea that intuitionistic logic is a solution to the problem of truth. In other words, intuitionistic logic has its own problem that is like the problem of truth. But I want to focus here on something a bit more ‘practical’. The gist of this more ‘practical’ issue, for me, has to do with my second question above: how does mathematics end up being helpful to humanity in a way that pure empirical reasoning isn’t? In Andrzej Grzegorczyk’s paper “ A Philosophically Plausible Formal Interpretation of Intuitionistic Logic “, Grzegorczyk interprets intuitionistic logic – logic without the law of the excluded middle – as the logic of empirical reasoning, and classical logic – logic with the law of the excluded middle – as a logic for metaphysical or ontological reasoning. (For those more serious logicians/mathematicians, this paper was one of the inspirations for Melvin Fitting’s/Raymond Smullyans intuitionistic interpretation of classical logic, and I think the fitting-smullyan view of classical logic as being what is recursively ‘necessarily possible’ in a kripke frame is extremely enticing for the view that classical logic is regulatory in the way that I will describe). Historically, intuitionistic logic is heavily inspired by the work of the imminent philosopher Immanuel Kant, who postulated the existence of an ‘intuitive’ aspect of the mind, and said that this part of the mind is the only source of absolutely true knowledge. Intuitionism takes this position seriously, and gets its name from this postulated faculty of the mind. But, I think this misses two crucial aspects of Kant’s philosophical position. I think a useful analogy here to understand this is a follows. Suppose there is a blind hiker who is trying to get to the highest peak in a mountain range. A blind hiker might feel around them and try to see where the terrain increases in height, and go in that direction. Eventually, they reach the highest peak on the current mountain this way, and realize there is no direction they can go without decreasing their elevation. Now, they could stop here, and simply assume they have found the highest peak. But in this simplified analogy, it’s extremely obvious that the blind hiker has no way of knowing if they have reached the highest peak or not. In particular, if this is all there was to it, the blind hiker might just stop, and never learn anything new about the terrain. In order to actually be sure, the blind hiker has to believe, at the very least, that there might be a higher peak out there somewhere, and go searching for it. In order to do so, they have to actually sacrifice some elevation first, before they reach the base of the current mountain and find the next. Now, maybe there is a higher peak, and maybe there isn’t, but in the process, the blind hiker discovers many new animals, plants, caves, rivers, and interesting other things (that are helpful) along the way, that they never would have discovered if they believed whole-heartedly that their current mountain was the only one. And, they might even discover a higher peak, as they hoped. It is in this sense, that the belief that there is a higher peak is ‘regulative’. It regulates the blind hiker’s search. It’s an incentive to act and stay focused, rather than simply stay put and never learn anything new. One might argue that the regulative belief is unnecessary because the hiker could go searching, but the existence of some regulative belief is necessary. I.e. if the hiker didnt have any regulative beliefs at all, then the blind hiker might either stay put like we mentioned before, or just e.g. choose random directions and eventually end up in the ocean, or back in some city, and not even care about exploring the mountain range. There is another aspect of this particular belief that is useful: the belief that there is a higher peak is ‘necessarily possible’: in other words, no matter how much information the hiker gets, its always possible for there to be a higher peak using their current methods of information gathering (assuming, as in the ‘ spherical cow ‘ that the terrain is infinite). This allows the hiker to never have to find some other regulatory activity. Here is where we return to my original question: how does mathematics end up being helpful to humanity in a way that pure empirical reasoning isn’t? In this same sense, if we think of scientific or empirical reasoning as it is like in Grzegorczyk’s paper, then scientific or empirical reasoning much like the hiker who only searches in their direct vicinity. This is of course useful, but it can’t be the only kind of thinking. In my opinion, mathematics distinguishes itself from science by concerning itself with ontological reasoning, which is regulatory for us as a species. And it distinguishes itself from philosophy at large in that it takes this ontological reality as a given. It takes the ultimate regulatory idea of mathematical truth as a given. It may be the case that the beliefs that come along with thinking of mathematics as ontological in nature are true, or it may be the case that they are false, but either way, they give us a means of searching beyond our direct vicinity, and finding out new things we never would have predicted we would find without getting lost (in the same way the blind hiker may not have predicted the discovery of a new species of animal: its not even what they were looking for!). In this exact way, if one uses AI as primarily a way to turn a large swath of mathematics into a purely empirical discipline (which is what happens if no mathematicians understand what is going on, and simply observe with their senses a ‘true/false’ verdict), then one loses the benefit of mathematics entirely. One has to use the ontological parts of mathematics, which can, in the above strange sense, only be carried out by humans, since otherwise it becomes purely empirical in nature in the sense of Grzegorczyk. Without this, we are very likely to miss out on discoveries we would have otherwise made. I want to make one last point about AI, since one might argue: well all that is well and good, but why isnt it the case that AI is simply a blind hiker as well, and has its own regulatory beliefs? Well, this may be true, but I would argue that we know it cannot be the specific regulatory belief mentioned above: that mathematics has an ontological status. This is because of Tarski’s undefinability theorem. The concept of mathematical truth cannot be defined, and so, since AI is just a computer program, it is definable in principle, and so is its search for mathematical truth.
